chapter_theme: Last songs at Thiruvannamalai (திருவருணை, 6 of 6): a life wasted by fate in women's craft that asks to reach the feet through Tamil song; a whole life traced from the drop in the womb to the pyre that leaves not a handful of ash; and a plea for the feet that are Jnana-Siva; the praise centres on Murugan coming on the peacock to the tower of Arunai, the hill of fire.

443.reading: The poet says that, as fate had it, his mind wavered in the craft of young women, his understanding turned and he wandered in deeds as a fool; he asks Murugan to come so that this displeasure ends and he may reach the feet in due order, thinking of them through the ancient great Tamil set to music. The praise names Kumaresa who fought the deceitful demons' crowns to the ground and whom all the worlds circle, fanned by the gods with chowries, who comes beautifully on the peacock to the tower of Arunai.
443.nuance: விதியதாகவே opens the confession by laying it to fate. முதிய மா தமிழ் இசையதாகவே மொழிசெய்து: the way to the feet is song in old Tamil. முனிவு தீர may mean the Lord's displeasure or the poet's own vexation.

444.reading: The poet traces a life from conception to the pyre: the drop in the womb, the whorl and the clot of blood, the growth month by month until birth in the tenth, the infant crying in its filth, at the breast and crawling, the decked child sent to learn, the youth following dancing women into lovemaking and spending his wealth, then disease and mockery, grey hair, the stick and a body bent like a monkey's, the wife taking charge of the goods, Death's noose dragging the life away, kin wailing each for their share, the drum, and the burning; he asks whether he should be this body, not worth even a handful of ash. The praise is a long battle in drum syllables, a catalogue of Siva's emblems and of Uma who bore Murugan, and his union with Devayanai and Valli, ending at the hill of fire, Arunai.
444.nuance: The plea runs as one sentence through every stage of life, each image piled on the last, until ஒருபிடி பொடிக்கும் இலை எனும் உடல், a body not worth a handful of ash. சந்தித்து அவரவர் பங்குக்கு அழுது: the kin weep, each for their share, and the wife has already taken the property (சம்பத்து ... அண்டைக் கொளுகையில்). In the praise Uma is given Siva's own emblems, the axe and deer in her hand and the dwarf Muyalakan under her foot (மழு உழை கரத்தி ... முயலக பதத்தி). Many lines of the embryo passage and of the battle are hard to divide.

445.reading: The poet describes women anointed with civet, rosewater and musk, with heavy breasts, scented cloud-dark hair and thread-thin waists, who lose all shame, and calls himself the fool who mixed with them and wandered, thinking what he sought was the goal; he asks for the feet that are Jnana-Siva. The praise names the feet on the peacock that turn devotees' deeds to ash, the son of Sivakami Uma who granted Kali her dance with Hara, the six-faced child of the river, who sported with Valli and married her, the nephew of victorious Raghurama, at ancient Arunapuri.
445.nuance: நாடியதுவே கதி எனா சுழலும் மோடன்: the error is taking the object of desire for the goal. ஞானசிவமான பதம்: the feet are not a means to knowledge but are knowledge and Siva. The line on Kali dancing with Hara appears to allude to their dance contest; how Uma's grace enters it is unclear.

links.note: Tirumular says the form grows ten months, comes into the world in its season and grows mingled with maya, and asks who knows how. 444 follows that same growth month by month to birth in the tenth, and then on past it to the pyre.
Both hear the funeral drum while kin wail over the corpse; the Naladiyar's drum mocks the living, while 444 notes that the kin weep each for their own share.

The song asks to reach the feet by speaking of them in old Tamil set to music (முதிய மா தமிழ் இசையதாகவே மொழிசெய்தே நினைந்திடுமாறு). Tirumular says the Lord made him well so that he would render the Lord well in Tamil (தன்னை நன்றாகத் தமிழ்செய்யுமாறே). Both poets treat making the god in Tamil as their own way to him, Tirumular as the purpose of his birth, Arunagiri as the remedy for a life misspent.

The song ends its life-story with the kin weeping each for their share (சந்தித்து அவரவர் பங்குக்கு அழுது), the drum, and the burning that leaves not a handful of ash. Tirumular's verse has the whole town wail (ஊரெலாம் கூடி ஒலிக்க அழுதிட்டு), rename the man a corpse, burn him and bathe and forget. Both close on the mourners rather than the dead man, and the song adds a motive Tirumular leaves out: the weeping is for the share.

The song asks for the feet that are Jnana-Siva (ஞானசிவமான பதம்), against the fool who took what he sought for the goal (நாடியதுவே கதி எனா). Tirumular says knowledge of the holy feet makes one Siva and is itself release (திருவடி ஞானம் சிவமாக்குவிக்கும் ... திருவடி ஞானமே திண்சித்தி முத்தியே). The song's compound names in one phrase what the Tirumanthiram verse unfolds line by line: the feet, knowledge and Siva as one goal.
